newsitem.title: USA: Signet redesign matches market expectations.
newsitem.headline: Signet redesign matches market expectations.

text.p: Signet Banking Corp revealed fresh details on the "redesign" of its business on Tuesday, but analysts said much of the plan had been expected.
"The reaction is disappointing in that all of the bank stocks (except Signet) are up," said one analyst.
Another analyst, who did not want to be identified, said the news was positive, but "it did not exceed expectations that had been in the market for a few weeks."

Signet said it would sell 39 of its 233 branches. Those locations, with deposits totaling $800 million, are in the "neck" of northern Virginia, southwest Virginia and on the Eastern Shore of Virginia and Maryland.

Analyst Moshe Orenbuch of Sanford C. Bernstein Co said Signet would have little difficulty finding buyers among smaller banks already operating in those areas. He estimated the branches could reap a premium of $60 to $70 million.
A Signet spokesman said J.P. Morgan & Co Inc has been hired to conduct the sale, and it is expected to close in six to nine months.

Richmond, Virginia-based Signet said it would concentrate its branch banking resources in an area stretching from Baltimore south to Washington through Richmond and east to the Hampton Roads area of Virgina.
That area is characterized by greater population density and a higher growth rate, Christopher Oddleifson, executive vice president for consumer financial services, said in a telephone interview.

The redesigned Signet will also concentrate on national financial services. For example, Oddleifson said, Signet has a national business specializing in lending to the media and helping media clients manage their balance sheets.
National consumer lending will involve products such as loan by check, installment loans, home equity loans, credit cards, mortgages and student loans in all 50 states.
Oddleifson said Signet was targeting 18 to 20 percent return on equity, which would put the company in the "top tier" of U.S. banks.
Commenting on the muted stock market reaction to the Signet plans, Orenbuch said "the bottom line is they are getting to a level of performance that most banks already are at when this is done."

Signet said the redesign -- called the Advance program -- would reduce expenses by $58 million net of implementation and technology costs, and add $10 million to revenue by the end of 1998. It said that was equivalent to a per-share annual "improvement" of $0.72 after tax.
It said the expense reducton would come from the creation of common functions across multiple business lines, a redesign of processes, automation and the integration of systems.
The redesign includes a $41 million technology investment.
Signet said it planned a second-quarter restructuring charge of $57 million pre-tax.

Signet also said its board of directors authorized a share repurchase program for up to five percent of the outstanding common shares. The repurchase plan is expected to be completed by the end of the year.

Orenbuch said he raised his 1998 earnings estimate to $2.80 per share from $2.60. He may also raise his 1997 estimate for operating earnings to $2.40 per share from $2.35. The analyst said he was keeping a buy rating on the stock "for now."
In addition to the 39 branches being sold, six branches are targeted for closing.

The plan will result in 327 layoffs and elimination of another 808 jobs through a hiring freeze, voluntary departures, attrition and sale of branches. At the end of 1996 Signet had a total workforce of about 5,000, including more thant 900 part-time employees.
Signet shares closed one point lower at 32-1/2 on Tuesday.
